headings.title: Introduction and Scope of Rehabilitation Facilities
headings.content:
Rehabilitation hospitals provide specialized, intensive care designed to restore functional independence to individuals recovering from debilitating illnesses, major surgeries, or severe trauma. Unlike acute care facilities focused on immediate medical stabilization, rehab units concentrate on maximizing residual physical, cognitive, and psychosocial capacities. Patients often arrive following cerebrovascular accidents, spinal cord injuries, complex orthopedic surgeries, or traumatic brain injuries.

In the Nigerian healthcare landscape, dedicated rehabilitation centres are relatively scarce, meaning many patients receive transitional therapy within general hospital wards or specialized outpatient clinics. Understanding the unique ecosystem of a rehab facility allows nursing students to appreciate the shift from curing disease to adapting to altered life capabilities.

headings.title: Core Objectives of Rehabilitation Nursing
headings.content:
Rehabilitation nursing centers on empowering patients to adapt to altered life roles through targeted interventions. The scope extends far beyond basic hygiene and medication administration. 

- **Restoration**: Rebuilding lost physiological and cognitive functions through consistent practice.
- **Prevention**: Guarding against secondary complications such as pressure injuries, deep vein thrombosis, and joint contractures.
- **Adaptation**: Teaching alternative methods for executing activities of daily living when full recovery is impossible.
- **Education**: Empowering both the patient and their family members to manage ongoing health needs independently.

headings.title: The Multidisciplinary Rehabilitation Team
headings.content:
Comprehensive rehabilitation requires synchronized collaboration among diverse healthcare professionals. No single discipline can address the complex, multifaceted deficits presented by patients with severe neurological or orthopedic impairments. 

| Discipline | Primary Focus |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Physiotherapy** | Gross motor skills, gait training, and musculoskeletal strength |
| **Occupational Therapy** | Fine motor skills, activities of daily living, and adaptive equipment |
| **Speech-Language Pathology** | Swallowing disorders (dysphagia) and expressive/receptive communication |
| **Medical Social Work** | Psychosocial support, discharge resources, and financial counseling |

As the professional who maintains continuous 24-hour contact with the patient, the nurse acts as the central coordinator, synthesizing inputs from all team members into a cohesive daily routine.

headings.title: Patient Assessment and Individualized Care Planning
headings.content:
Effective rehabilitation begins with a rigorous baseline assessment that evaluates what the patient can still accomplish independently alongside their specific deficits. Standardized tools, such as the **Functional Independence Measure (FIM)** or the **Barthel Index**, quantify a patient's level of disability in areas like self-care, sphincter control, mobility, and communication.

Nursing assessments must look beyond physical metrics to evaluate psychological readiness, cognitive processing, and home environmental constraints. Care plans are dynamic documents, updated regularly during interdisciplinary team conferences to reflect incremental milestones or setbacks. Setting realistic, patient-centered goals prevents frustration and fosters continuous motivation.

headings.title: Management of Chronic Conditions and Functional Deficits
headings.content:
Patients admitted to rehab units frequently manage coexisting chronic illnesses such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease alongside their primary disability. Nurses must balance active rehabilitation exercises with rigorous physiological monitoring. 

Fatigue, pain, and spasticity often impede participation in therapy sessions. Proactive pain management and scheduled rest periods are essential nursing interventions. Furthermore, nurses monitor for orthostatic hypotension during early mobilization attempts, ensuring safety by utilizing gradual positional changes and compression stockings.

headings.title: Transition of Care and Community Integration
headings.content:
Discharge planning in rehabilitation is not a terminal event executed on the final day; rather, it is a continuous process that begins upon admission. Preparing a patient for return to the community requires evaluating the home environment, organizing necessary durable medical equipment, and training family caregivers.

In many Nigerian communities, limited infrastructure, architectural barriers, and cultural perceptions regarding disability present profound reintegration challenges. Nurses must connect patients with local support groups, outpatient therapy clinics, and home-care resources to ensure continuity of care and prevent avoidable hospital readmissions.
